Identifying knowledge gaps and learning opportunities with AI: Why it matters

Why use AI to identifying knowledge gaps and learning opportunities?

Student data is everywhere, whether it's LMS activity logs, quiz results, course evaluations or advising notes. However, making sense of it in a meaningful and timely way can be overwhelming. Too often, we rely on "lagging indicators"  like final grades or end-of-semester feedback to identify student challenges, by which point it may be too late to intervene effectively.

A metric that reflects past economic, business or financial events, providing insight into the effects of past actions. This term is being used in an educational context.

Generative AI can help surface patterns in student performance and engagement data that might otherwise go unnoticed. With the right prompts, these tools can detect where students are struggling, where they’re disengaged and where support might make the biggest difference.

Regardless of your role in students' lives, learning to analyze data early and intentionally helps create more equitable, proactive and student-centered strategies across roles.

Identifying knowledge gaps and learning opportunities with AI: How it works

Identifying knowledge gaps and learning opportunities with AI: How it works

Qualitative and quantitative data often hold signals about student understanding, motivation and experience but they aren’t always easy to interpret at scale.

Quantitative Data

These data types are often collected automatically and give measurable insights into student behavior and performance.

  • LMS analytics (log-ins, time-on-task)
  • Quiz scores or assignment completion
  • Attendance or submission timestamps

Qualitative Data

These forms of data offer rich insight into student thinking, emotion and experience often in their own words.

  • Discussion board comments
  • Open-ended survey responses
  • Advising summaries or case notes

All this data can provide incredibly valuable insights into drop-off points in a course, repeated misunderstandings in assignments or unengaged learner groups. It can also reveal what's going really well for students. Generative AI tools can play an important role in pulling these insights out so they're useful to you.

 

How can AI help? 

Generative AI's ability to process, interpret and summarize large amounts of student data can reveal patterns that might otherwise be buried in spreadsheets, a survey platform or long blocks of text. Select each analysis use case below to learn more!

Repeated misconceptions in assignments

AI can analyze open-ended student responses or rubric-aligned grading data to flag concepts that are frequently misunderstood. This allows instructors or designers to revisit content or provide targeted clarification.

Emotional tone in written feedback

AI can detect whether students express frustration, satisfaction, confusion or motivation in their written responses (like surveys or discussions). This gives insight into student experience that goes beyond grades.

Participation trends over time

AI can process LMS or activity logs to reveal when students engage—or disengage—most. These trends can inform changes to pacing, support outreach or assignment design.

Drop-off points in engagement or performance

AI can pinpoint moments in the course where many students stop submitting work, log in less or experience performance declines. These “drop-off” points are valuable opportunities for timely intervention.

 

Prompting AI for student insights

What you get out of AI is only as good as what you put in, so specifying what you're prompting for is key.

 Summarization condenses long text into key points, helping you quickly understand what students are saying in free-form survey responses or discussion forums.

  • “Summarize the key themes in these discussion board posts from Week 3. What are students most focused on, and are there signs of confusion around specific concepts?”
  • “Summarize the most common concerns and needs expressed in these advising case notes from the past month.”

 Clustering groups similar student responses or behaviors into categories (e.g., similar concerns about workload, or confusion around a topic), which can guide support strategy or redesign.

“Can you group these open-ended course evaluation responses into 3–5 categories based on recurring themes, such as clarity of instruction, workload or support availability.”

 Sentiment analysis uses language modeling to infer whether feedback is positive, negative or neutral. It can help you understand the overall mood or morale of your students, especially in response to instructional changes.

  • “Analyze the tone of these mid-course feedback responses. Which comments express positive sentiment, which express negative sentiment and what topics are tied to each?”
  • “Identify the emotional tone in these anonymous student reflections from an orientation program. Are students expressing excitement, concern or confusion?”

 Pattern detection identifies recurring behaviors or data points like consistent lateness, missed deadlines or topics that produce more questions. This can prompt deeper inquiry or guide immediate tweaks to learning design or support outreach.

“Review this spreadsheet of quiz scores and time-on-task data. Identify any trends in performance drop-offs, missed assignments or reduced engagement over time.”

Identifying knowledge gaps and learning opportunities with AI: Professional connections

Connect to your context

Read the scenario below and take a moment to reflect on how it might be relevant to your context.

Janelle | Academic Success Coach

Lately, Janelle has noticed a troubling trend: several students in her caseload are failing their general education courses, but not because of missing work. They’re attending class, logging into the LMS and completing assignments on time. When Janelle meets with them, they express confusion and frustration. “I thought I was doing okay,” one student tells her. “Then I saw my midterm grade and I was shocked.”

Janelle wants to better understand where these students are struggling and why their engagement isn’t translating into academic success. Her institution recently rolled out access to a generative AI tool that can analyze de-identified data, including LMS logs, short-answer quiz responses and advising summaries. She decides to explore whether these tools can help her detect learning gaps or disconnects in understanding that she and her students might not be seeing.

But she’s hesitant. Can she trust the AI to interpret tone or trends in student writing?
